To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we introduce a novel collaborative causal discovery problem, and (ii) under a clustering assumption we give an algorithm that requires only a logarithmic number of atomic interventions to learn all causal graphs simultaneously.

we introduce a novel problem called Collaborative Causal Discover and show that it can be solved with significantly fewer atomic interventions than the number of atomic interventions required to learn each of the $M$ causal graphs independently.

we can collaboratively learn all the causal models in a cluster of entities using significantly fewer interventions than the number of interventions required to learn each individual model separately.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: 1) What can we learn about a collection of causal models if we can perform interventions in a collaborative manner? 2) How many interventions do we need to perform to do so?
the following questions: 1) What is the minimal amount of intervention required to recover all underlying causal graphs of multiple independent entities?

understanding the benefits of collaborative causal discovery, and the interplay between the clustering property of the underlying causal graphs and the number of interventions required to recover them.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in our collaborative setting, if we are able to perform a logarithmic number of interventions per node in each entity, then we are able to recover the causal graph of all entities simultaneously.

our work provides a novel approach for causal inference in a collaborative setting, where we can learn all the underlying causal graphs with a number of atomic interventions that is logarithmic in the number of entities, and is independent of the number of observable vertices in the causal graphs.

we show the first algorithmic result for collaborative causal discovery, which is also the first work to show that causal discovery can be done using fewer interventions than the number of nodes in the causal graphs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that collaborative interventions can be used to learn all causal graphs in the setting of MAGs with significantly fewer number of interventions.

we show how to leverage clustering of causal graphs to reduce the number of interventions needed for learning the graphs, and how to leverage clustering across entities to reduce the number in collaborative causal discovery.
we show the power of collaboration in learning the causal graphs, which is especially important when the causal graphs are large and the entities have limited access to the data.
The main takeaway from our work is that

by sharing interventions, one can significantly reduce the sample complexity for causal discovery, and that the sample complexity of causal discovery is significantly lower than the sample complexity of learning the underlying causal graph structure.

, in a collaborative causal discovery setting, we can leverage the fact that all the entities are working on the same problem to reduce the amount of interventions required to learn the causal graphs.

, when multiple independent entities are involved in the same causal discovery task, the ability to collaborate and actively perform atomic interventions allows us to significantly reduce the number of required interventions, compared to the standard causal discovery problem.
